Adam Stenavich.blurb: Stenavich's offense doesn't have a loud signature — nearly every schematic dial sits at or near league average, from play-action to tempo to screens. The one thing that stands out is restraint in the passing game, running slightly more than expected in a pass-heavy league. What the numbers do show clearly is results: +0.06 EPA/play ranks 14th, well above the league average of -0.01, which suggests execution is doing more work here than scheme novelty.

Andy Reid.blurb: Reid throws more than almost anyone — sixth-most pass-heavy offense in the league over this stretch — and leans on RPOs (4%, double the league average) and screens (10% vs. 7%) to keep defenses honest at the line. Pre-snap motion runs a bit above average at 48% but isn't the cornerstone it is elsewhere. The scheme value sits in the middle of the pack (-0.017 vs. -0.013 league average), meaning the results (+0.07 EPA/play, top 13) are more about execution than design — which, with this roster, is a reasonable trade.

Ben Johnson.blurb: Ben Johnson's system doesn't stand out for being exotic — his creativity score sits right at the league median — but the results are elite: +0.101 scheme value (fourth in the league) and +0.09 EPA/play, both well above average. The real structural signature is play-action at 25% against an 18% norm, paired with a tempo that runs about seven plays per game faster than league average. He runs a nearly run-first pass distribution and almost never uses RPOs, which makes the efficiency numbers more impressive, not less.

Brian Schottenheimer.blurb: Schottenheimer runs one of the more structurally conventional offenses in the league — creativity sits at 44, motion, play-action, and RPO usage are all right at league average — but the system is quietly producing. Scheme value of +0.077 ranks seventh of 76 callers, well clear of the league average of -0.013, which means the design is generating real QB- and opponent-adjusted value without leaning on exotic wrinkles to do it. The honest read: this is an execution-based system that earns its results through sound structure, not novelty.

Drew Petzing.blurb: Petzing runs one of the more conventional schemes in the league — creativity scores at 41, well below the league average of 50, and almost every other dial sits right at the norm. What he does do is lean slightly more on play-action than most (22% vs. an 18% average), and the results are quietly solid: +0.04 EPA/play against a league average of -0.01. Nothing exotic here, but the execution has been good enough to land above average on outcomes.

Jim Bob Cooter.blurb: Cooter's offense leans on play-action (22%, against a league norm of 18%) and touches RPOs at a slightly elevated rate, but beyond those two wrinkles this is a fairly conventional operation — motion, tempo, screen rate, and overall creativity all sit at or near league average. The results match the profile: -0.02 EPA/play, essentially league average and nothing that stands out in either direction.

Kellen Moore.blurb: Moore's system is about as close to the middle of the distribution as you'll find — conventional pass tendency, average play-action, average creativity, average results. The one thing that genuinely stands out is pre-snap motion at 48% of dropbacks, well above the ~40% league norm, suggesting the offense does its work manipulating defenses before the snap rather than through structural wrinkles. Tempo is a modest separator too, at 80 plays per game versus a 75-play average. Otherwise, this is a system still searching for an edge.

Kevin O'Connell.blurb: O'Connell's offense is essentially average across the board — pass tendency, motion, tempo, screens, and RPOs all sit right at league norms — with one meaningful exception: play-action at 23%, well above the 18% league average. The problem is it hasn't translated into results, with EPA/play at -0.06 against a league average of -0.01, and scheme value slightly below average at -0.042. The play-action lean is real, but the system hasn't been generating much off of it.

Kyle Shanahan.blurb: Shanahan's system sits near the top of the league in scheme value (+0.125, second of 76) and EPA (+0.14, fourth), and almost nothing about the design is exotic — creativity lands right at the league median. The one real structural tell is pre-snap motion, which he deploys on 59% of dropbacks against a ~40% league norm; that's the engine. Play-action, RPOs, tempo, and screens are all ordinary by design, which means the results come almost entirely from execution and pre-snap manipulation rather than schematic novelty.

Matt LaFleur.blurb: LaFleur sits middle of the pack on almost every schematic dial — motion, play-action, tempo, screen rate all near league average — yet ranks third in scheme value among 76 play-callers, which means the edge is coming from execution and design quality, not exoticness. He does run RPOs at a slightly elevated rate (3% vs. 2% league norm) and leans mildly run-heavy relative to expectation, but neither is the story. The story is that a conventional-looking system is producing elite QB-adjusted value, and that's actually harder to do than it looks.

Matt Nagy.blurb: Nagy's Giants offense runs a little pass-heavy — third-highest pass rate over expectation in the league — and leans on RPOs at roughly twice the league average (4% vs. 2%). Beyond that, the profile is mostly average across the board: creativity, motion, tempo, play-action all sit right around the norm. The results are slightly positive, which is a reasonable outcome for a scheme that isn't trying to win on cleverness.

Mike LaFleur.blurb: LaFleur's system doesn't stand out on paper — conventional creativity, ordinary tempo, no RPOs to speak of — but pre-snap motion at 52% of dropbacks is a genuine calling card, running well above the ~40% league norm and serving as the primary mechanism for creating leverage before the snap. Everything else sits close to average, and the offense has still produced above-league EPA, which suggests the motion-heavy approach is doing real work even when the rest of the scheme is unremarkable.

Mike McDaniel.blurb: McDaniel runs one of the more structurally unusual offenses in the league — pre-snap motion on 59% of dropbacks (league norm is ~40%) and screens at roughly 10% of plays combine to make defenses move and react before the snap as much as after it. What's harder to square is that he's also one of the run-heaviest callers in the data, sitting 5.1 points below expected pass rate, which cuts against the reputation for exotic design. The scheme grades out slightly below average on adjusted value, and results bear that out.

Sean McVay.blurb: McVay's system earns its value through process, not novelty — his creativity score sits below the league average, but the scheme grades out at +0.061, well above the norm. The signature levers are pre-snap motion (53% of snaps, against a ~40% league average) and play-action (23% vs. 18%), both used well above average to manufacture leverage before the ball is snapped. RPOs are essentially absent at 1%. The results — +0.06 EPA/play — back a system built on execution and structural advantage rather than exotic design.

Sean Payton.blurb: Payton runs a genuinely varied attack — screens at 10% and RPOs at 3% both sit well above league norms, and his creativity score of 58 lands in the top 15 among all play-callers — but the results so far in Denver have been middling, with EPA/play at -0.02 and scheme value only modestly above average. Pre-snap motion is actually below the league norm at 34% versus 40%, so the exoticness comes from play design and menu width rather than pre-snap manipulation. A scheme that looks more interesting on paper than it's delivered on the field, at least to this point.

Shane Steichen.blurb: Steichen's offense doesn't stand out on the surface — motion, tempo, screens, and pass tendency all sit right at or near league average — but the system is generating genuine value where it counts. His scheme value of +0.051 ranks ninth in the league against a negative league average, meaning the structure itself is producing above expectations after adjusting for quarterback and opponent. The one meaningful structural lean is play-action at 22% against an 18% norm, a modest but consistent commitment. Results so far in Indianapolis are middling at -0.02 EPA/play, which is an honest caveat — the scheme has upside the outcomes haven't yet reflected.

Todd Monken.blurb: Monken's scheme in Cleveland doesn't stand out on any structural dimension — motion, tempo, play-action, RPO usage, and screen rate all sit exactly at league average. What stands out is that it works anyway: his scheme value ranks tenth among 76 play-callers at +0.051, well above the league average of -0.013, and the offense produces +0.06 EPA/play against a league average of -0.01. The read here is execution over invention — a conventional framework that's generating real value above what the personnel alone would explain.

Wes Phillips.blurb: Phillips runs a mostly conventional offense — tempo, motion, RPOs, and screens all sit right at league average, and his creativity score lands exactly at the median. The one real differentiator is play-action, which he deploys on 23% of dropbacks against an 18% league norm, a genuine lean. The results haven't backed it up, though: -0.06 EPA/play ranks 54th, a meaningful gap below the league average of -0.01.

Zac Taylor.blurb: Taylor runs one of the most pass-heavy systems in the league — +8.0 over expected, second among all play-callers — and almost everything else sits right at the league norm: motion at 40%, RPOs at 2%, screens at 7%, tempo ordinary. The creativity score (40/100, well below the 50 average) confirms this isn't a scheme that tries to manufacture edges through exoticness; it leans on volume and execution. The results are solidly positive at +0.04 EPA/play, though the scheme value itself (+0.034) lands around the middle of the pack — which means the passing volume is carrying more weight than the design.

Bobby Slowik.blurb: Slowik runs one of the more structurally creative offenses in the league — 59/100 on exoticness, genuinely in the top tier — but the results haven't matched the design, with EPA/play at -0.06 against a league average of -0.01 and scheme value sitting at -0.081. The most defining quirk is how run-heavy he skews: -4.2 pass rate over expected puts him near the bottom of the league, well below the -0.8 norm. Pre-snap motion at 47% is a real commitment, but everything else — play-action, tempo, screens — is essentially average.

Brad Idzik.blurb: Idzik runs one of the most conventional offensive systems in the league — nearly every dial sits at or within a tick of league average, from tempo and play-action to RPOs and screen rate. The one thing that does stand out is pre-snap motion at 31%, meaningfully below the 40% norm, so defenses aren't getting a lot of conflict generated before the snap. Results land just above average at +0.01 EPA/play, which is about right for a scheme that wins on execution rather than design.

Dan Pitcher.blurb: Pitcher's system is about as conventional as it gets structurally — motion, tempo, RPOs, and screens all sit right at league average — but the defining characteristic is an aggressive pass-lean that ranks third in the league at +7.8 over expected, against a norm of -0.8. That's not situational; that's a philosophy. Play-action is actually below average at 14%, so this isn't a deception-based passing game — it's just a commitment to throwing it. The offense has produced a positive EPA/play, which is more than most can say.

Frank Smith.blurb: Frank Smith's offense is defined by two things above almost everyone else in the league: pre-snap motion on 70% of dropbacks (league average is 40%, and no one ranks higher) and a screen rate of 13% against a 7% norm, second in the league. Layer in play-action at 25% — well above the 18% average — and you have a system built on manufacturing stress before and after the snap. Pass tendency and tempo are ordinary, and the results land right around league average, so the pre-snap complexity isn't translating into a clear EPA edge yet.

Joe Brady.blurb: Brady's system stands out for two things that don't often go together: it ranks second in creativity league-wide, with pre-snap motion on 50% of dropbacks against a 40% norm, yet nearly everything else — play-action, RPO, tempo, screen rate — sits right at league average. The exotic elements are structural, not scattered across the whole menu. Scheme value is a modest middle-of-the-pack +0.025, but the offensive EPA of +0.18 per play is second in the league, which suggests the results are real even if the system itself isn't doing all the lifting.

Joe Lombardi.blurb: Lombardi's Denver offense leans on a few tools more heavily than most — play-action at 24% (league avg 18%), screens at 12% (more than double the 7% norm), and RPOs at 4% against a 2% average — which earns the scheme a legitimately high creativity score without being exotic for its own sake. Pre-snap motion and pass tendency both sit close to league average, so this isn't a system built on disguise or aggression; it's built on specific constraint-stressing concepts used at real volume. The results were dead even at +0.00 EPA/play, which is fine but not an endorsement.

Klint Kubiak.blurb: Kubiak's system is about as close to baseline as it gets — creativity, tempo, play-action, and screens all sit right at league average, and his pass tendency runs only marginally run-heavier than the norm. The one thing that stands out is pre-snap motion at 48%, meaningfully above the 40% league average, suggesting he uses formation manipulation as a primary diagnostic tool before the snap. Scheme value comes in at +0.019 against a league average of -0.013, and results land near even — a functional, if unspectacular, operation.

Liam Coen.blurb: Coen's offense doesn't stand out on any single structural dimension — motion, tempo, play-action, RPO usage, and screens all land right at league average. What stands out is the output: +0.10 EPA/play and +0.098 scheme value both rank fifth in the sample, meaning he's squeezing genuine production out of a conventional framework. The case for Coen is execution and design quality, not exoticness.

Nathaniel Hackett.blurb: Hackett runs one of the most conventional offensive schemes in the league — pre-snap motion at 28% against a 40% norm, play-action below average, RPOs nearly nonexistent, everything else sitting at the median. The creativity score of 36/100 ranks 72nd of 76 play-callers, so there's no exotic wrinkle to point to. What makes that concerning is the results: -0.10 EPA/play against a league average of -0.01, ranking 63rd, suggests the straightforward approach isn't being executed well enough to justify its simplicity.

Press Taylor.blurb: Taylor's system doesn't stand out on the surface — creativity, motion, play-action, and tempo all sit right around league average — but the scheme itself grades out well, +0.035 scheme value against a league average of -0.013, good for 13th among 76 callers. The one concrete outlier is pre-snap motion at 31%, notably below the ~40% league norm. The results are essentially neutral at -0.02 EPA/play, which is roughly where the league sits, so the scheme value hasn't fully translated yet.

Zac Robinson.blurb: Robinson runs one of the more run-heavy systems in the league — passing 5.7% less than expected, well below the -0.8 league norm — but the results don't validate the approach, with EPA/play sitting below average and scheme value at -0.068 against a league average of -0.013. The one wrinkle worth noting is pre-snap motion at 48%, modestly above the 40% norm. Otherwise this is a conventional, low-creativity system that hasn't yet earned its conservatism.

Alex Van Pelt.blurb: Van Pelt's New England offense runs faster than anyone in the league — 86 plays per game against a 75-play average, and it's not particularly close. Everything else sits at or near league norms: conventional structure, average motion, average play-action, screens slightly elevated at 9%. The pace hasn't translated to production, though; at -0.11 EPA/play, the results rank near the bottom of the league, and scheme value comes in below average as well.

Arthur Smith.blurb: Smith runs a run-heavy offense — passing 3.5 fewer times per game than expected, well below the league norm of roughly even — built around two genuine wrinkles: play-action at 23% (league avg 18%) and screens at 10% (league avg 7%). Those aren't unrelated; the run commitment creates the leverage that makes both work. The results land exactly at league average EPA/play, which is honest: this is a functional, execution-first system that generates a little above-average scheme value without doing anything exotic.

Declan Doyle.blurb: Doyle runs one of the more creative offensive systems in the league — 63rd percentile on exoticness, fifth overall — but the surface call sheet looks conventional: play-action, motion, tempo, and RPO usage all sit right around league average. What actually sets him apart is scheme value: +0.081 against a league average of -0.013, sixth overall, meaning he's consistently generating advantages before the results even come in. The offense is delivering too, at +0.10 EPA/play, so the creativity isn't decorative — it's working.

Doug Nussmeier.blurb: Nussmeier runs a straightforward offense — conventional tempo, average motion and pass rate, almost no RPOs — and the one dimension that stands out is what's missing: play-action at 13% and screens at 3% are both well below league norms of 18% and 7%. That's a scheme that doesn't lean on constraint plays, which is a legitimate philosophy, though the -0.07 EPA/play suggests it hasn't fully paid off yet. Worth noting he's currently in an OC role without play-calling duties.

Eric Bieniemy.blurb: Bieniemy's Washington offense passed at one of the highest rates in the league — +7.0 over expected, a top-4 mark — while running notably less pre-snap motion (28% vs. a 40% norm) and slower tempo than most. The creativity score of 57 suggests genuine structural variety despite that minimalist operation, though scheme value came in near league average and results were middling. A pass-heavy system that moved the ball adequately but didn't generate a real edge.

Grant Udinski.blurb: Udinski's Jacksonville offense doesn't stand out for anything exotic — creativity, motion, play-action, and screens all sit right around league average — but it passes more than almost anyone would expect given the situation, running +2.8 over expected pass rate against a league norm of -0.8. The pace is deliberately slow at 72 plays per game, one of the lower marks in the league. What makes it work is the production: +0.09 EPA/play, eighth-best among 76 play-callers, which suggests the choices, conventional as they look, are consistently the right ones.

Greg Roman.blurb: Roman's system has two genuine signatures: play-action on 27% of dropbacks — second in the league against an 18% norm — and pre-snap motion on 52% of snaps, well above the 40% average. Everything else sits near the middle: creativity at 48 (league average is 50), screens and RPOs both negligible, tempo ordinary. The play-action volume is the defining bet, and the results so far are modest — +0.01 EPA/play, right around league average.

Josh McDaniels.blurb: McDaniels runs one of the most conventional-looking offenses in the league — near-average motion, play-action, and tempo, almost no screens or RPOs — and yet his scheme value ranks first among 76 play-callers after adjusting for quarterback and opponent. The gap between how unremarkable the profile looks and how much the system actually produces is the whole story: this is execution-based offense, and the results (+0.10 EPA/play, sixth overall) back it up.

Ken Dorsey.blurb: Dorsey's clearest fingerprint is pace — 85 plays per game ranks second in the league against a norm of 75, and he pairs that with a pass-lean that sits comfortably above average. Everything else is genuinely ordinary: motion, play-action, screens, and RPOs all land right at the league mean. The problem is the results don't vindicate the tempo emphasis — scheme value comes in at -0.093 against a league average of -0.013, and EPA/play is negative, suggesting the volume isn't generating much.

Klay Kubiak.blurb: Kubiak runs a pass-heavy offense — +3.4 over expected, well above the league's -0.8 baseline — with virtually no RPOs (0%, compared to a 2% norm) and below-average tempo at 68 plays per game. The structure is deliberate and conventional in most respects, but it produced +0.15 EPA/play, third-best in the league. The results say the scheme doesn't need to be exotic to work.

Klayton Adams.blurb: Adams runs one of the most conventional offensive schemes in the league — nearly every structural lever sits exactly at league average, and screens are the one notable outlier, coming in at 4% against a 7% norm. What stands out isn't the design, it's the output: +0.09 EPA/play ranks 9th across all 76 play-callers, well above the league average of -0.01. Sometimes the most honest read is that the execution is doing the heavy lifting.

Kliff Kingsbury.blurb: Kingsbury's system in Washington runs at genuine volume — 82 plays per game against a league average of 75 — and layers in play-action at 26% (league average is 18%, top-3 in the sample) and RPOs at 4% (nearly double the norm), which together explain most of the elite creativity score of 64/100. The scheme value sits at +0.048 against a league average of -0.013, and the offense has produced +0.07 EPA/play, so the exoticness isn't just cosmetic. Pre-snap motion is above average but not a defining feature; the identity is really built on structural deception before and after the snap, run at a high clip.

Luke Getsy.blurb: Getsy runs a genuinely up-tempo offense — 83 plays per game ranks eighth in the league against an average of 75 — and pairs that with pre-snap motion on 51% of dropbacks, well above the ~40% norm, suggesting a system built around creating defensive conflict before the snap. Everything else sits near league average: play-action, screens, RPOs, pass tendency. The problem is the results: -0.10 EPA/play against a league average of -0.01 is a real gap, and scheme value of -0.052 versus -0.013 average means the system itself isn't generating much edge independent of personnel.

Mike Kafka.blurb: Kafka's scheme reads as almost perfectly average across the board — creativity, motion, play-action, RPOs, and screens all sit right at league norms — with one real outlier: he runs fast, ranking 9th in tempo at 83 plays per game against a league average of 75. The problem is that pace hasn't produced anything; at -0.14 EPA/play, the offense ranks 72nd of 76, and his scheme value of -0.138 sits well below the league average of -0.013. More snaps, worse results.

Mike McCarthy.blurb: McCarthy passes more than almost any play-caller in the league — +3.6 over expected, ninth-highest — but does so with almost no play-action (12%, against an 18% league norm), which is an unusual combination. The rest of the scheme is conventional across the board: average motion, tempo, screens, and creativity scores all cluster near the mean. The results haven't justified the approach: -0.09 EPA/play ranks 62nd, a meaningful gap below average even after adjusting for quarterback and opponent.

Nick Caley.blurb: Caley's Houston offense is about as close to league-average as it gets across nearly every structural dimension — motion, tempo, play-action, and pass tendency all land within a point or two of the norm. The one real outlier is screens, where he calls them at 3% against a 7% league average, one of the lowest rates in the league. Results are modestly positive at +0.01 EPA/play, though scheme value sits just below average at -0.025, suggesting the production is more player-driven than system-driven.

Nick Holz.blurb: Holz runs a run-heavy, conventional offense — nearly everything here sits at league average except his pass rate, which is 6.5 points below expected, the fourth-lowest in the league. That's a philosophical commitment, not an accident. The problem is it isn't working: -0.14 EPA/play ranks 71st of 76, and his scheme value of -0.110 against a league average of -0.013 suggests the design itself isn't generating much lift beyond the personnel.

Shane Waldron.blurb: Waldron's scheme is unremarkable in almost every dimension — creativity, motion, play-action, and pass tendency all sit right at or near league average — with one real outlier: a screen rate of 12%, nearly double the league norm of 7% and fourth-highest among all play-callers. That's a deliberate strategic lean, not noise. The results have been below average (-0.03 EPA/play against a league norm of -0.01), though how much of that is scheme versus roster is a fair question.

Tim Kelly.blurb: Kelly runs a run-heavy attack — 4.3 points below expected passing rate, well below the league norm of -0.8 — built around play-action (24% vs. 18% league average) and screens (10% vs. 7%) to manufacture easy throws off that run commitment. He plays fast, pushing 82 plays per game against a 75-play norm, which compounds the volume. The results are middling (-0.02 EPA/play, roughly league average), and the scheme value is similarly unremarkable, so the identity is clear even if the outcomes aren't yet convincing.

Tommy Rees.blurb: Rees runs one of the most run-heavy offenses in the league — passing nearly 7 fewer times per game than expected, with zero RPO usage against a 2% league norm — and the pace reflects that same conservatism at 70 plays per game versus a league average of 75. The rest of the scheme sits squarely at league average across motion, play-action, and creativity. The problem is the results: -0.12 EPA/play ranks 68th of 76, which is the kind of number that doesn't hide behind a philosophical commitment to the run.

Andrew Janocko.blurb: Janocko runs one of the more stripped-down offenses in the league — almost no play-action (8% against an 18% norm), minimal motion (22% vs. 40%), essentially zero RPOs, and a slow pace that ranks near the bottom. The creativity score reflects all of that. What keeps it from being a knock is the EPA: +0.02 per play, above league average, suggests the simplicity is at least executing.

Brian Angelichio.blurb: Angelichio runs a stripped-down passing offense — almost no play-action (7% against an 18% league norm), virtually no motion (18% vs. 40%), and zero RPOs — but leans heavily pass despite all of it, sitting sixth in pass rate over expected at +5.5. The result is an offense that telegraphs its intentions and generated below-average EPA at -0.08 per play. Straightforward by design, but the execution didn't hold up the bet.

Brian Daboll.blurb: Daboll's offense in Tennessee runs about as lean as any in the league — 17% pre-snap motion against a ~40% norm, screens on just 2% of plays versus a 7% average, and a pace of 53 plays per game that ranked dead last. The stripped-down approach might be a philosophical choice, but the results don't give it cover: -0.15 EPA/play against a league average of -0.01, near the bottom of all tracked coordinators.

Brian Fleury.blurb: Fleury runs one of the slowest, most stripped-down offenses in the league — 62 plays per game against a 75-play norm, no RPOs, 12% play-action against an 18% average, and pre-snap motion at 25% when most teams are near 40%. The creativity score sits right at league average, which makes sense: this isn't an exotic system, it's a deliberately minimal one. The problem is the results don't yet justify the restraint — scheme value and EPA/play are both below average.

Chip Kelly.blurb: Kelly's offense in Las Vegas runs heavy pre-snap motion (56%, against a ~40% league norm) and leans on play-action at one of the highest rates in the league (25% vs. 18% average) — the structural hallmarks of his system are genuinely there. The problem is the results: -0.21 EPA/play ranked dead last among the 76 coaches in this sample, and a scheme value of -0.177 confirms the system itself isn't generating edge independent of personnel. The motion and play-action are real, but they aren't working.

Dave Canales.blurb: Canales runs a largely conventional offense — creativity, motion, pass tendency, and screens all sit right at league average — with one notable outlier: RPOs on 4% of plays, well above the 2% norm and a top-ten rate league-wide. Play-action at 22% is a modest uptick from average, and his tempo is slightly up-tempo at 81 plays per game. The scheme value is positive but modest, and the results land just below average at -0.02 EPA/play — a middle-of-the-road picture overall.

David Blough.blurb: Blough's offense is one of the most stripped-down in the league — virtually no RPOs, almost no screens (2% against a 7% norm), and pre-snap motion at 20% when most teams are running it on 40% of snaps. Play-action is similarly absent at 8% versus an 18% average. The results land right at league average EPA, so the minimalism isn't hurting him, but the scheme value sits in the middle of the pack — this is execution-dependent football with very few schematic levers built in.

Davis Webb.blurb: Webb's Denver offense was defined more by what it didn't do than what it did — play-action at 9% against a league average of 18%, pre-snap motion at 23% against 40%, screens at 4% against 7%, and a tempo of 57 plays per game that ranked 75th of 76. That's a slow, stripped-down operation across the board, not a philosophical minimalism so much as a constrained one, and the -0.08 EPA/play reflects it.

Frank Reich.blurb: Reich's Jets offense is about as bare-bones as it gets — pre-snap motion at 14% (league average is 40%), play-action at 8% (league average 18%), and screens at 2% (league average 7%) all rank near the dead bottom of the league, making this one of the most static, unadorned systems in football. That's not inherently a problem, but the results don't vindicate the minimalism either: -0.03 EPA/play sits below the league average, and scheme value is essentially neutral at -0.002.

John Morton.blurb: Morton runs one of the least exotic offenses in the league — 38th percentile on creativity, rarely passes over expectation — but the underlying structure is anything but vanilla. He leans heavily on pre-snap motion (59% of dropbacks, against a ~40% league norm) and play-action (26%, fourth in the league vs. an 18% average), runs screens at a high clip, and keeps tempo up near the top of the league. The results back it up: +0.08 EPA/play and a scheme value well above average, built on execution and structure rather than complexity.

Josh Grizzard.blurb: Grizzard runs a high-volume, motion-heavy offense that separates itself from the pack in a few specific ways: pre-snap motion on 58% of dropbacks (league norm is around 40%) and screens at nearly double the average rate (10% vs. 7%) pair with a pace of 84 plays per game, sixth-fastest in the sample. Beyond those three levers, though, it's a conventional operation — pass tendency, play-action, and RPOs all sit right at league average. The results reflect that: EPA/play is league-average, and scheme value comes in slightly below it.

Kevin Patullo.blurb: Patullo runs one of the more structurally active offenses in the league — pre-snap motion on 52% of dropbacks (league avg ~40%) and a creativity score of 62/100 that ranks sixth overall — without leaning on tempo or screens to manufacture it. The rest of the profile is fairly conventional: pass tendency, play-action, and pace all sit near league average. Results are modestly positive at +0.03 EPA/play, though scheme value comes in below average at -0.031, meaning the complexity is generating outcomes more than the system itself is.

Nathan Scheelhaase.blurb: Scheelhaase runs one of the more stripped-down systems in the league — almost no motion (25% vs. a 40% norm), no RPOs, barely any screens, and low play-action usage — but he leans heavily toward passing, sitting at +4.4 over expected pass rate against a league average of -0.8. The results are modestly positive at +0.04 EPA/play, so the minimalist approach isn't hurting him, though one season of data keeps the verdict tentative.

Pete Carmichael Jr..blurb: Carmichael's Buffalo offense is one of the more unusual profiles in the data: a creativity score of 83 — first among 76 coordinators, well clear of the league average of 50 — built almost entirely without the tools most offenses lean on.
